props.title: Last Man Standing
props.initialSlug: Lone gunman plays rival gangs in Prohibition Texas

sections.content: Last Man Standing (1996) represents Walter Hill's gritty Prohibition-era reimagining of Akira Kurosawa's Yojimbo (1961), following Bruce Willis as John Smith, a gunman who plays rival gangs against each other in a dusty Texas border town. The film builds on a fascinating cinematic lineage - Kurosawa's samurai classic inspired Sergio Leone's A Fistful of Dollars (1964), which then influenced Hill's neo-noir western. Willis brings his trademark smirk and world-weary charm to the role, while Christopher Walken delivers a memorably menacing performance as hired gun Hickey.

sections.content: The film's style merges classic western tropes with Prohibition-era gangster elements, creating a unique hybrid that would influence later genre-blending films like Road to Perdition (2002). Hill's direction emphasizes brutal violence and moral ambiguity, hallmarks of both western and noir traditions. The film's dusty Texas setting recalls earlier westerns like Once Upon a Time in the West (1968), while its organized crime elements echo gangster classics like Miller's Crossing (1990). SUBHEAD: Neo-Noir Western Evolution

Last Man Standing sits at an interesting crossroads of 1990s genre revival, alongside films like Unforgiven (1992) and Tombstone (1993). These films brought contemporary sensibilities to traditional western frameworks, often incorporating elements of noir and modern action cinema. The film's violence is stylized and brutal, with Hill utilizing Willis's action star persona developed in Die Hard (1988) while grounding it in a period setting.
